prime.problem: Picking uniformly from [0, n) minus a blacklist by drawing again until allowed needs n / m calls on average, with no worst-case bound: 10⁵ calls per pick if all but 10 of 10⁶ values are banned. Listing every allowed value costs O(n) memory.
prime.fits: Follows the LFU cache in Coding and design. It reuses the Big-O card's dense-range trick (RandomizedCollection's swap with last) and a dict from the hashing card, applied once in a constructor instead of on every removal.
expect: m = n − (number banned): the size of the draw range
fillers: allowed values at or above m
prime.goal: Build a sampler that uses one random call per pick in O(1), prove it's exactly uniform by showing the draw range maps one-to-one onto the allowed values, and choose it over rejection sampling or a sorted blacklist when it fits.

attend: Why are there always exactly as many holes below m as fillers at or above m?
Why must the filler walk go down from n − 1 and skip banned values?
What makes the picks exactly uniform, not just approximately?
Why does top only ever move down, and what does that do to the build cost?
When is plain rejection sampling the better choice?

must: Only m = n − b values are allowed → draw from [0, m) and nothing else → one random call per pick

Banned values below m are holes; allowed values ≥ m are fillers → counts match (both equal b minus the banned values ≥ m) → map each hole to a distinct filler → every draw lands on a distinct allowed value → a bijection, so each is picked with probability exactly 1/m
The filler pointer top only moves down, skipping banned values → it passes each banned value at most once → O(b) build, O(b) memory, O(1) per pick

Rejection costs n / m calls on average (1.75 here, 1.752 measured) → cheap when few values are banned (1 / 0.99 ≈ 1.01 at 1%) → the remap wins when most values are banned or a worst-case bound matters
elevated: A chi-square test checks a histogram against uniform (1.26 on 3 degrees of freedom, p = 0.74 here) → it can only fail to find bias, never prove its absence → the bijection check on 1,000 random cases is the real proof
reference: the closed-form chi-square tail for 3 degrees of freedom
the source's Java storing every banned value in its map with a dummy 1
the alias method for weighted picks
the binary-search alternative with O(log b) picks

compress.prompt: From memory, draw 0…6 with 2, 3, 5 banned, mark m, the holes and the fillers, and write the remap. Then explain in 3 sentences why one random call per pick is exactly uniform.
checklist: the draws 0, 1, 2, 3 map to 0, 1, 6, 4: every allowed value exactly once
a bijection from [0, m) onto the allowed values gives probability 1/m each
build O(b), pick O(1), memory O(b)

retrieve.q: Explain why the number of holes always equals the number of fillers.
answer: there are n − m = b values at or above m, of which some are banned
holes = banned values below m = b − (banned ≥ m)
so the counts match and every hole gets its own filler

retrieve.q: Walk through the constructor for n = 7, blacklist = [2, 3, 5].
answer: 2 < 4 is a hole: 6 is allowed, remap 2 → 6, top = 5
3 is a hole: 5 is banned, skip to 4, remap 3 → 4, top = 3
5 ≥ m is never drawn: nothing to do

retrieve.q: The blacklist changes between picks. What happens to the remap, and which alternative handles updates better?
answer: a new ban can create a hole or remove a filler, breaking the pairing
so the dict must be rebuilt, O(b) per change
a sorted blacklist with binary search for the k-th allowed value handles inserts better, at O(log b) per pick

compare.q: Both cards keep a dense range so one random index is a pick. When does each fill the hole, and what does each remember to do it?
answer: RandomizedCollection fills a hole at every remove by moving the last item into it
the blacklist card fills all holes once, in the constructor
RandomizedCollection needs value → set of positions to find and move items
the blacklist card needs only hole → filler, O(b) memory

compare.q: Uniform-with-exclusions vs weighted picks: what does each precompute so that one draw is O(1), and when would you switch from this card's remap to the alias method?
answer: remap: a bijection from [0, m) onto allowed values; every allowed value has weight 1
alias: a table of n columns, each split between at most two outcomes, so non-uniform weights also need one draw plus one coin
switch when values have unequal probabilities
both pay O(size) up front for O(1) per pick

predict.q: Build the sampler for n = 6, blacklist = [0, 1, 2]. Before running: what is m, what is the remap, and what fraction of draws get remapped?
predict.answer: m = 3 and remap = {0: 5, 1: 4, 2: 3}. Every value in the draw range is banned, so all draws are remapped: 100%. The pick is still one random call and exactly uniform over 3, 4 and 5.

apply.task: Trace the constructor for n = 10, blacklist = [1, 4, 8, 9] by hand (m, each hole, each filler and the skips). Then compute the expected number of random calls per pick for rejection sampling on this input, and check both with the code.
apply.done: m = 6, remap = {1: 7, 4: 6} (9 and 8 are skipped on the way down), and rejection needs 10 / 6 ≈ 1.67 calls per pick on average against exactly 1 for the remap.
apply.hint: 8 and 9 are banned but ≥ m, so they are never holes, only values the filler walk skips.
